Pet Brands Find New Ways to Invite the Family Dog to Thanksgiving Dinner

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adweek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2023, pet information site Veterinarians.org polled 1,000 dog owners and discovered that 68% planned on making a Thanksgiving meal just for them.
  • Sources indicate that think that’s a lot?
  • Premium pet-food brand Ollie recently surveyed 1,000 dog owners and found that, as the holidays approach, 96% of dog households blueprint to prepare Rover “something special to eat.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2023, pet information site Veterinarians.org polled 1,000 dog owners and discovered that 68% planned on making a Thanksgiving meal just for them.

Sources indicate that think that’s a lot? This year, that number is closer to nearly all of them.

Premium pet-food brand Ollie recently surveyed 1,000 dog owners and found that, as the holidays approach, 96% of dog households blueprint to prepare Rover “something special to eat.”.

Few are more aware of this shift than pet brands, which are rolling out Thanksgiving-specific products and promotions to help consumers include dogs at the dinner table—at times literally.

According to recent reports, ollie—which sits in the fresh, human-grade dog food category—is offering a Holiday Feast meal made with traditional Thanksgiving ingredients like turkey, cranberries, and sweet potatoes. On Nov. 21 and 22, select Petco stores hosted Petsgiving, a cooking lesson on how to cook a dog-appropriate Thanksgiving meal.

“These are the latest in our series of retail-tainment events designed to create opportunities for connection and bonding between pets and pet parents,” Petco’s SVP of brand creative Alison Hiatt told ADWEEK.

According to recent reports, in a similar bid to “let dogs join in Thanksgiving,” legacy pet food brand Purina recently announced a limited edition run of its Beggin’ line of treats in flavors like Bacon ’n Turkey and Honey ’n Ham. Just Food for Dogs is selling its limited-run Thanksgiving Feast Recipe online this year for the first time.

And to promote its limited-time Harvest Turkey dinners, premium brand Maev has released its “Seat at the Table” campaign that presents dogs “as respected guests of honor at the Thanksgiving table.”.

“We’re in the midst of a fundamental shift in the role dogs play in our lives, from existing on the periphery of our identity to becoming an extension of it,” mentioned Maev’s senior director of brand Maddy Tank. “We’re increasingly bringing them into the rituals, routines and experiences that make us human.”.

Holiday promos are nothing newly introduced, of course, but why the concerted effort now to give dogs a place at the Thanksgiving table? It’s a combination of several forces.

First, more people own dogs. In 2025, dog ownership in America rose from 51% to 53%, according to the American Pet Products Association. Most of that growth is coming from zoomers and millennials, and these are the generations most likely to regard a pet as a full-fledged family member—by rates of 68% and 69%, respectively, according to Euromonitor data.

Sources indicate that “There are also fewer people having children,” Ollie CMO Allison Stadd told ADWEEK. “So dogs are increasingly filling that role that people might have filled with human children in the past.”.

Even among families with children, Purina senior brand manager John Paul Vella added, “dogs have been elevated to child status among consumers.”.

Finally, there’s a growing awareness that feeding fido scraps from the Thanksgiving table can actually be harmful, a concern that opens the door to these specialty meals and offerings.

Some of which can be extremely special. Ollie automatically enrolled everyone who bought its Holiday Feast online before Nov. 3 in a drawing to win a $1,700 Baccarat crystal bowl—for the dog, of course.

Robert Klara is the senior editor of brands at Adweek, specializing in the evolution and impact of brands.

Recent findings suggest that as a Senior Server Engineer on Foundations you'll drive server architecture modernization and build the AI tooling the whole eng team uses. Small team, huge surface area. ~80% roadmap, ~20% keeping the lights on. Node.js + TypeScript at consumer scale.

The ideal candidate has 5+ years of experience, has been the technical leader on past teams, thinks like an owner, builds with AI (not just alongside it), and would rather fix it for everyone than just for themselves.

We offer comprehensive medical and dental coverage, $50 a day food delivery budget, equity based employment, a great culture, learning opportunities, unlimited vacation, 12 weeks paid parental leave, and we pay all employees $1,000 a year to go somewhere in the world that they've never been because of our values of human connection, empathy, and curiosity.

Platform Ownership: Collaborate, build, and lead key components of the shared foundation every Raya engineering team builds on: AI infrastructure (LLM gateway, model routing, spend tracking, code review agents), server architecture, shared libraries, developer tooling, and CI.

Architecture: Drive server architecture modernization. Write the tech specs, make the trade-offs ourselves, plan the work so it ships safely, and see it through to adoption across engineering!

AI Tooling: Build and roll out the AI-collaborative development tooling Raya engineers use every day, from model routing and eval harnesses to cloud agents that review code and catch slop, and set the standards for how we use it.

Engineering Standards: Set the bar the rest of engineering follows through design reviews, code review, and the docs that let other teams build with confidence.

Operational Excellence: Own the full Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) for what you build: CI/CD, observability and alarm coverage, security remediation, and a healthy, blameless on-call rotation. Be an escalation point for deep production debugging.

Mentorship: Help engineers grow through pairing, code review, and direct feedback.

5+ years of hands-on experience building and operating production server software, with a track record of delivering scalable and maintainable systems and growing into a technical leader within your organization.

Demonstrated expertise in system design, architecture, and mastery in Node.js and TypeScript.

Proven experience in building and scaling backend systems in production at a startup or fast-moving environment.

Hands-on with MongoDB and/or PostgreSQL in production, including performance tuning.

Experience owning platform, infrastructure, or developer-productivity work that other teams depend on (shared libraries, CI/CD, dev tooling, observability, or security remediation) and driving its adoption.

Has built and shipped products with LLMs or AI agents in production, beyond a chat wrapper.

Enthusiasm around latest AI tools and frameworks - and a willingness to quickly adopt emerging best practices.

Modernizer: You've led a large architecture migration across a codebase other teams depend on, and you got it adopted.

AI Infrastructure: Experience with LiteLLM, Amazon Bedrock, or similar model-routing layers, and with prompt engineering, evals, or fine-tuning in production.

Infrastructure-fluent: Comfortable with AWS, Docker/Kubernetes, and CI/CD, and with the security & infra side of running a consumer product at scale.

Tech Report: Future of Marketing Briefing: Consulting firms revive their marketing ambitions in the C-suite the holdcos covet

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
  • This Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m.
  • However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

This Future of Marketing Briefing covers the latest in marketing for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Friday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

However the holdcos settle the question of whether the CEO route counts as due diligence, Deloitte Digital and Accenture Song got there first, and both have started selling marketing in the C-suite with a fresh push.

In a recent development, deloitte Digital’s offer is Converge, an operating system that strings together AI agents to run marketing and sales work, from research and briefs through to campaign deployment and deal tracking. Some of the agents are Deloitte’s own. Others are ones a client already runs elsewhere, and the whole thing plugs into the tools and clout contracts a brand is already paying for. Marketing and sales versions are live, with commerce on the way, and Deloitte pitches them as one front-office system tied to revenue, which it calls “brand to cash.” Because it’s sold as a license that stretches across sales, marketing and service, it needs sign-off well above the CMO, which suits a consulting firm that’s used to having those conversations.

Accenture Song’s play in media, a market it has circled in the U.S. for years without committing. In September, it moved Melissa Fein, who built its media planning and buying business in Australia and New Zealand after leaving Initiative in 2024, to New York as U.S. media lead. This month it posted a job for a head of media strategy for the Americas. The ad describes a “new world media practice” with no legacy systems to protect, and asks for an AI-first strategist” to lead planning, build new tools and become the person senior clients call before a brief exists.

Candidates need hands-on command of econometrics, incrementality testing and attribution plus experience in significant-spending categories like financial services, telecommunications, automotive and health. Those are the categories where the ANZ team won Australia Post and Mediabank. Accenture Song Ndidi Oteh has kept quiet on specifics, saying only that whatever it does in media won’t take traditional forms.

Recent findings suggest that “The real prize is the conversation before the brief,” stated  Steve Boehler, founder of agency consultancy the Mercer Island Group. ”If you help define the business problem, design the operating model and decide how success will be measured, you are competing long before an agency review begins.”.

It has been revealed that both plays echo what the holdcos have spent 18 months engineering: operating systems that run a client’s marketing for it and media businesses that sell more than buying. The consultants may have the better shot at making either one stick. They already sit with the CEOs, CIOs and CFOs who sign off on systems spanning sales, marketing and service and installing that kind of software is their day job. A holdco operating system, rightly or wrongly, still reads as an agency tool, built partly to make the agency cheaper to run. Accenture also arrives in the U.S. media with no legacy buying business to protect, so it can lead with measurement and tools before it has to sell buying power.

Whether any of this translates is another matter. Consultancies have been trying to crack advertising for the best part of a decade, after all, and the media buying business still rewards a scale Accenture doesn’t yet have in the U.S. Then again, now is arguably as good a time as any for them to try, if not better. With Omnicom and IPG combined, massive advertisers are down to three holdcos, and some are skipping the pitch one so a credible alternative has rarely been more useful. AI is also pushing decisions about how marketing works into rooms where the CFO and CIO sit, which consultancies have been in for years. And a C-suite that takes a closer look at marketing will start asking how agencies make their money, from data fees to principal media, which is an awkward question for any firm with a buying business to defend.

“The consultancies may have an advantage in getting invited to design the system,” said Boehler. “That is not the same as proving they can run marketing better. The client still needs evidence of better decisions, better work and better business outcomes, not just fewer handoffs.”.

Industry observers note that all of which makes the Publicis-WPP episode look a little quaint, partly because it was never quite the fight it was billed as. Sadoun spent months telling investors that Publicis was winning big accounts without a pitch. Rose, asked about it by an analyst, called it “this pitchless CEO handshake thing that I keep getting asked about” and said decisions that big deserve careful consideration. Publicis answered with an open letter treating that line as her theory, and the coverage did the rest. Somewhere along the way, a question about how clients choose agencies turned into a row about manners.

It has been revealed that what got lost was the shift both CEOs were describing. Substantial advertisers are increasingly buying data, identity and AI infrastructure, which a six-week parade of slide decks was never built to judge, so some now test one partner in depth instead of auditioning several. Those decisions are also moving up the organization chart, to executives who sign off on systems not campaigns. That’s how consultancies have always been bought. Deloitte and Accenture are built for long, technical evaluations run by CFOs and CIOs, and while the holdcos; remarks were being turned into a grudge march one debuted a system that needs the c-suite’s signature and the other started building a U.S. media practice designed to win it.

“Client CEOs and CMOs pay attention to CEOs of holdcos, especially when a transition in agency leadership occurs and the agency CEO conducts outreach to key clients,” mentioned Gartner analyst Jay Wilson. “But most recognize that while agency CEOs may set a direction for the agency, that direction may be slow to take hold – or never take hold – within the agency teams doing the actual day-to- day work. A strong relationship with, or aversion to, an agency chief executive is usually more consequential at smaller, independent agencies.”.

Whatever gets agreed in the c-suite, someone still has to do the work.

“The consultants don’t have to copy the incumbent model to compete,” stated Boehler. “But they still have to do the work: strategy, negotiate, deliver, reconcile and prove results. A different model is a proposition until clients experience the difference.”.

In a recent development, cinema admissions have climbed back on the strength of a fuller blockbuster slate and much of the ad money that shifted to digital during lockdowns stayed put. Most screens still sell their preshow through sales houses that have always sold offline.

According to recent reports, mikkel Hagedorn, a WPP and Omnicom alum, has spent five or six years building a platform that lets buyers book cinema spots programmatically, target them against specific films and count impressions straight off ticket sales. The firm is live in Denmark and Finland, where sales houses have handed it two minutes of a 15-minute preshow at a base CPM of around €75. Hagedorn’s bet is that exhibitors can bring cinema into the digital ad market while keeping the premium pricing newspapers gave away when they went programmatic.

His manufacturer, called Cinemataztic, gives buyers two ways to purchase inventory: first, agencies already running programmatic campaigns can reach the inventory through supply-side platforms and demand-side platforms such as Smartclip Google’s DV360 respectively, which lets cinema sit inside budgets that were going to be spread across other channels anyway, Advertisers who would rather skip the intermediary fees can book directly through Hagedorn’s own interface.

Recent findings suggest that either way, the buyer can pick what individual film they want to target, so a brand could run only against the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday movie if it likes. The impressions they buy come straight from exhibitors’ ticketing systems, which means one ticket sold counts as one impression. There are “no multipliers here,” noted Hagedorn, a dig at the audience multipliers that inflate numbers elsewhere in media.

So far a lot of the money has come from digital agencies edging up the funnel into brand work. Hagedorn remarked he has seen little cannibalisation of advertisers still buying cinema the old way. He said the business has grown 50% a year and forecasts the same for next year, when the company expands into Sweden, Thailand and a third, bigger market he wouldn’t share.

Recent findings suggest that even so, the programmatication of cinema will be a slow burn. Advertising is still its third-largest revenue line after tickets and concessions. Most hand it entirely to sales houses on contracts of three to five years and only learn that demand is falling when the next guarantee shrinks. Hagedorn has been warning them about this for years. “They cannot stay offline forever,” he remarked.

Brands that gatecrash cultural moments tend to stick to tournaments and royal weddings, and they rarely pick a game that lets players mug strangers in a fake Florida. Grand Theft Auto, the culture-warping franchise, is the exception, and its sixth installment is drawing the kind of guerilla marketing normally reserved for FIFA and the Olympics.

Anyone trying to keep up can follow the running tally at GTA6Brands.com, an independent tracker run by Mike Litman that logs a fresh stunt each day for his GTA 6 Marketing News podcast. Hardly anything in culture still sets off that kind of scramble across so many brands at once, and with GTA the explanation is scale.

According to recent reports, “I’ve tracked over 290 brand moves around GTA 6 so far, including around 130 unofficial activations,” stated Litman. “That’s a remarkable amount of marketing activity orbiting a product launch, particularly when so many of those brands have no formal relationship with Rockstar. What’s interesting is the range of brands getting involved.”.

It has been revealed that with media this fragmented, marketers have a shortlist of moments when a mass audience demonstrates up at the same time, and most of those moments involve a ball. GTA earned its spot on that list over 13 years. When GTA 5 launched in 2013 it made $1 billion in three days, which owner Take Two called a rate faster than any other video game, film or other entertainment product has ever managed. For context, Marvel’s “The Avengers” movie took 19 days to reach that number. In the years since it launched, the game has since surpassed 230 million units sold worldwide across three console generations. The wait for the sequel turned into an event of its own. GTA 6’s second trailer received 475 million views across all platforms within 24 hours of its release, beating the 365 million in 24 hours for Marvel’s Deadpool & Wolverine film. Take Two has issued $8 billion for its 2027 guidance for the fiscal year the game releases in. For a brand that wants a crowd all watching the same thing at once, that’s about as close to a World Cup final as entertainment gets, and nobody has to get past FIFA’s lawyers.

“I think the fascinating thing is that GTA 6 has achieved something usually reserved for the World Cup or Super Bowl, but without the stadium, the broadcast rights or the traditional sponsorship machinery,” said Litman. “It’s become a cultural event in its own right. And brands aren’t waiting for permission to participate.”.

Recent findings suggest that A few did get permission, though. Rockstar’s list of official partners is short and made up mostly of platforms. Sony signed an exclusive marketing deal, which put a “Plays Best on PS5” tag on the game’s official channels. Netflix got the “Extended Look” trailer six trailers before YouTube in August, in what Take Two boss Strauss Zelnick called a “groundbreaking partnership”. YouTube is running a 24-hour launch live livestream from its own channel, and the Miami Heat have redesigned court, custom uniforms and Vice City merchandise.

It has been revealed that “Nike is going back to its roots and what built the brand: cultural relevance through people who have the trust of a community. It is a bold choice when most advertising pitches are about AI. Nike uses AI too, as a tool, but clearly demonstrates it understands that what stays scarce is trust. Trust comes from identity and proximity: who is speaking, and how close they are to the community listening. It also shows what creators and athletes must build to ask a brand like Nike for more than just a campaign fee. Most of them are offering access to an audience that belongs to a social or tech platform, targeted and measured with the data that the platform makes available. Global stars aside, only those who directly own the relationship with their audience and their data can negotiate a share of the long-term value.”.

— Alessandro De Zanche, founder of media consultancy ADZ Strategies on Nike’s bet on creators to drive growth.

$70.7 million: The total amount that U.S. advertisers spent on ChatGPT ads during October.

$83: The initial share price for Anthropic when the organization went public.

It has been revealed that $24.6 billion: The total that U.S. B2B digital ad spend is expected to reach by the end of 2026.

$1.65 billion: Total in pre-order sales ahead of the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 launch.

Meta Testing New Prediction-Market App With EmployeesMeta staff are testing Takes, an internal prediction-market app where people bet points called “cred” instead of real money, and there’s no word yet on a public launch, per The Wall Street Journal.

Amazon is paying to reach ChatGPT shoppers while the chatbot is finding other ways to surface its products and deals.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that this Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m.
  • Sources indicate that so many surprises came out of the midterm elections, and only one of them was the rout by Democrats over Republicans on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Recent findings suggest that this Media Buying Briefing covers the latest in agency news and media buying for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Monday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

Sources indicate that so many surprises came out of the midterm elections, and only one of them was the rout by Democrats over Republicans on Nov. 3 and in the days following.

There’s a lot to be unpacked as to what impact the $12.06 billion spent during the 2025-2026 election cycle had, according to AdImpact’s revised numbers post-election, but let’s start with the fact that the outlay was the most of any cycle on record and $460 million (4%) more than AdImpact’s last projection in June.

It’s also the first time a midterm election outspent a presidential election — which only portends even more to be spent in 2028’s presidential race.

In a recent development, why did Republicans fare so poorly when they outspent Democrat candidates overall? According to AdImpact, Republican candidates dropped $5.51 billion, a 27% hike over the 2024 cycle, compared to Dems’ $5.11 billion, which actually represented a 4% drop.

It has been revealed that in light of that, it’s fair to ask whether political advertising still delivers the same impact and effect on voters as it had in a simpler media environment. More specifically, is TV still the way to influence voters? The answer leans toward no, since TV still attracted the most dollars, with both broadcast and streaming growing their ad dollars.

Recent findings suggest that “Reaching voters and engaging them are two different things. Ads build awareness. On their own, they don’t persuade anyone or get them to the polls,” noted Travis Trawick, CEO of FullPAC, a nonpartisan political technology firm. “The shift is from talking at voters to talking with them. The technology exists today to have two-way conversations at scale, see what’s landing and feed it straight back into strategy while there’s still time to act on it.”.

It has been revealed that the numbers generally support that tech-forward approach. Looking again at post-election AdImpact data, broadcast TV set a record $5.85 billion, up 9% from 2024, as its share of spend edged up from 48% to 49%. CTV rose 14% to $2.66 billion, while digital media rose 11% to $1.91 billion. Media losing share included cable (−7%), radio (−13%), and satellite (−7%).

Sources indicate that but what about the hottest thing in media buying right now, creators? Political candidates turned to them heavily in this cycle. Newly introduced research from creator marketing firm Kyra, which works with SharkNinja, H&M and L’Oréal to run influencer campaigns across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, showed a strong swing in influence for Democratic-leaning creators. D-leaning creator posts drew 329.9 million views from 923 posts by 146 creators, while Republican-leaning ones drew 37 million from 170 posts by 27 creators — about 9 to 1 in views and 5 to 1 in posts.

(One crucial caveat that Kyra noted in its research: its YouTube data is “thin [with 9.9 million views], and we don’t cover X, podcasts, Rumble or long-form YouTube, where right-leaning creators are widely thought to be stronger.”).

Recent findings suggest that political ad tech firms are noticing that influence. “When you can have trusted messengers really resonating with an audience, whether you’re trying to sell a product or convince someone to vote for a candidate, having that trusted messenger is really a powerful thing,” explained Mark Jablonowski, CEO of DSPolitical, an ad-tech firm that works with candidates mostly on the Democratic side of the aisle. “Having the social sphere of people responding to the news and clipping and sharing in a very organic and viral way is an vital thing.”.

Jablonowski said Republicans have historically utilized the MAGA network of influencers much more effectively in the past. “This was one of the first years that Democrats really spent significant resources and time on focusing on this, and it was definitely a component of their success,” he said, although he argued that the critical problems of broken promises, war and inflation had the single largest effect on the voter swing —far more than any media strategy had.

It has been revealed that there’s little doubt even more ad dollars will be poured into the next presidential election than we witnessed this year. And it will start sooner than ever, with 2027 possibly enjoying more of a windfall of primary spending than any off-year, mentioned Jablonowski. He cited local down ballot races as contributing to that expected increase.

“When we’re looking to 2028, we’re going to see more of these advanced technologies being attainable by the down ballot races,” he said. “You’re just going to see all of the local races really utilizing this best in class tech because it is available and consumable.”.

FullPAC’s Trawick agreed that 2028 will break all the records that have been set before in every election cycle, presidential or midterm. “The question is whether campaigns keep spending the same way,” he saod. “They shouldn’t. 2027 and 2028 call for a different approach, and it starts with the calendar. The campaigns that win will plan earlier: introduce the candidate, build relationships and test messages long before broadcast rates spike.”.

Industry observers note that as far as preferred media, Jablonowski expects to see not only more CTV/streaming and creator investment by candidates, but also digital audio/streaming. “The plumbing has finally been plumbed in, where you can address audiences at scale through streaming audio, whether it be podcast or or music,” he said.

StackAdapt’s political team, in an email to Digiday, said its expects well-funded presidential candidates could start buying ads to build name recognition as early as Q2 or Q3 next year, depending on when they enter the race.

Expect to see TV, particularly linear, used less and in different ways. “Money follows what can be measured. We can expect to see more spending on channels that reach a specific voter and show you whether it worked: texting, CTV and streaming and targeted digital,” said Trawick. “Broadcast won’t disappear, but late-cycle saturation gets harder to justify. Three weeks of TV at peak rates, aimed at people who already voted early, is the first line item that should get a hard look. The bigger shift is the calendar, not the channel. Early voting turned election day into a season, and budgets have to be built for the whole season.”.

There’s really only one set of numbers that was crucial last week: sales of Grand Theft Auto’s 6th installment. According to Sensor Tower (numbers that have not yet been confirmed by Rockstar Games) pre-orders and first-day sales exceeded 24.5 million copies, generating approximately $2.36 billion. It’s widely considered one of the biggest entertainment blockbusters in any medium ever. So, if your brand isn’t too worried about brand safety or adjacency to hardcore content, maybe GTA 7, whenever that comes out, is the place to be.

“John was one of the rare ones that could negotiate an entire marketplace — including sports, and he knew everything about the sports marketplace — but didn’t have to just be a specialist … with John leaving the business, we are going to be missing one of the true intellectual hearts of the buying side.”.

Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

Advertisers continue to increase investments on the retail weekend but AI, tariffs and discounting pressure present banana skins.

Hybrid won the in-housing debate, at least among the largest advertisers

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
  • Reports of the media agency’s death remain greatly exaggerated.
  • Advertisers are carving up the media operation with more intent, keeping the work that sits closest to the brand and handing the sprawling specialist stuff back to their agencies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Reports of the media agency’s death remain greatly exaggerated. Its job description, however, is another story.

Advertisers are carving up the media operation with more intent, keeping the work that sits closest to the brand and handing the sprawling specialist stuff back to their agencies.

The shift has been playing out in fits and starts for the best part of a decade. COMvergence’s first Global Advertiser Survey reveals how far its got. The media agency research firm polled 28 senior marketing, media, procurement and operations leaders at 21 global advertisers, who between them control more than $22 billion in media spend. A quarter of them buy or control media in-house. Of the rest, around a third are thinking about bringing spend in-house over the next 12 months.

“It’s a bit like a football club,” noted Jon Williams, founder and chief creative officer at Freedom Works, a collective of senior agency execs who help brands build in-house teams. “You build your own academy and you’re proud of it. You still buy a striker when you need goals. You just don’t keep a dozen agents on the payroll in case.”.

According to recent reports, whether they’ve started in-housing or are still weighing it up, few advertisers want to take everything off their agency’s plate. Most would rather divide the work. Nearly 80% of respondents described their setup as hybrid, mixing internal teams with agency support. Fewer than 18% run media entirely in-house.

Industry observers note that “The CMO isn’t always the one pushing,” remarked Scott Grenz, head of U.S. operations for COMvergence. “Much of the energy comes from internal media, procurement and data/analytics teams. They believe owning their data and getting full transparency are key to media effectiveness, and that often leads to bringing parts of the digital media scope in-house.

“Agencies have become more transparent, and advertisers are looking at their media ecosystem as a whole, asking how best to use all their resources, internal and external, to hit their critical KPIs, mentioned Grenz.

Which is to say the motive for in-housing has moved from saving money to getting better at specific things. Mars is staffing internal teams to get ready for agentic shopping, while Gap has gone as far as setting up its own entertainment studio. Lego brought programmatic in-house partly so it could make better informed calls on which ad tech vendors to use. Its agency, and its vendors, can expect sharper questions as a result.

“When I started out, the in-house studio was where ads went to get resized,” mentioned Williams. “The agency did the thinking and the studio did the cutdowns. Nobody would say that now.”.

It has been revealed that getting here took the best part of a decade. For most of that time, in-housing was a cost and transparency play with advertisers chasing cheaper media and a clearer view of where the money went. The ANA’s 2016 report on agency rebates gave plenty of them reason to look. Somewhere along the way, the question moved on to what their own teams could do faster or better.

In-house teams tend to go where the budgets are, which for most advertisers means digital. The largest group of respondents put 60% to 70% of total media spend into digital and plenty go higher, according to the report. Only a very small minority keep digital below 30%.

Unsurprisingly, social media is where advertisers are most willing to take the wheel. More than 85% of the in house operators in the survey run social themselves. Search display and programmatic trail at roughly 57%. The logic is simple enough. Social rewards fast decisions and direct access to audience data, both of which come easier when the team sits inside the business.

In a recent development, the same can’t be noted of retail media, CTV and influencer marketing. They remain mostly agency-run, with relatively few advertisers taking them on directly. All three are fragmented and specialized enough to keep agencies in demand. Take Retail media. Its sprawl of networks and measurement approaches is the sort of mess advertisers seem happy to pay someone else to untangle. Several respondents still named influencer, commerce and retail media as where they’re experimenting with upcoming models or looking for outside guidance.

“Building an in-house media practice is hard. It carries real risk, takes significant resources and requires capabilities many advertisers don’t have yet,” remarked Grenz.” Still, there are plenty of use cases across the industry, from big advertisers and small, and no single model has won out. Our data shows that many advertisers who have in-housed still work with a media agency. That’s the real takeaway: it isn’t all or nothing. Advertisers are working out the right mix of internal and external expertise to make their media effective.”.

For all the talk of brands doing more on their own, agency rosters remain crowded. More than half (54) of the marketers COMvergence interviewed use more than one media agency and more than half bring in digital specialist agencies alongside their main one.

Still, that crowding probably won’t last. More than 80% of the advertisers working with multiple agencies strategy to simplify or consolidate. They want specialist expertise and fewer partners at the same time — a tension that should keep the pitch consultants busy for a while.

Sources indicate that “Some of it is procurement,” said Williams. “One in-house lead told us it took nine months to get a newly introduced supplier set up. Do that ten times and you’ll consolidate too. And AI is taking away a lot of the everyday work that used to keep four or five agencies busy.”.

Half of the respondents use global hubs, offshore resources or both. Their comments pointed to India, Colombia, Brazil, Mexico and other regional centers, mostly handling digital operations, programmatic buying, social execution and support work.

Recent findings suggest that advertisers see these setups as agency-run rather than as their own teams. That’s a handy calling card for holdcos selling scale. In fact, COMvergence expects hubs and offshore talent to become an even bigger differentiator for agencies as labor costs rise and more execution gets automated.

Industry observers note that “There’s no universal ceiling,” noted Grenz. “It comes down to how each advertiser weighs the risk and reward of in-housing against agency management. Agencies have made a strong case that they’re a critical partner, and they’ve shown they’re willing to work within whatever hybrid model a client wants.”.

Asked what they’d like more of, respondents pointed squarely at agency operating models, which made up more than 40% of all feedback. They want to see how peers structure internal teams, split work between brand and agency, govern media investment and run in-house functions.

It has been revealed that the usual caveats apply to a report like this. Twenty one advertisers is a small sample so a handful of companies can swing a percentage by a lot. COMvergence plans to run the survey every year and the second edition should say more about the direction of travel than this first snapshot can.

Even so, the findings are a good encapsulation of how senior marketers at the largest advertisers see where things are headed.

Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

Advertisers continue to increase investments on the retail weekend but AI, tariffs and discounting pressure present banana skins.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moving from CMO to Chief Revenue Officer changes the questions you ask (and which numbers keep you up at night).

In this episode of Marketing Vanguard, Jenny Rooney sits down with Kathy Collins, Senior Vice President and Chief Revenue Officer at Frontdoor, to unpack what happens when a career built in marketing expands into sales, finance and full revenue accountability.

Kathy shares how cross-category experience sharpened her ability to find the right audience and make unfamiliar products relevant, why she became “obsessed with numbers” and what leading sales taught her about communication.

Plus, her candid thoughts on why curiosity matters more than comfort.

Kathy Collins is Senior Vice President and Chief Revenue Officer at Frontdoor, where she started as Chief Marketing Officer. Today, her role brings marketing, sales and revenue thinking much closer together.

Her career has spanned several major consumer brands and categories, including Lee Jeans, H&R Block and Massage Envy, before she joined Frontdoor.

That current broader scope of her work has also changed how she approaches marketing, from a stronger focus on unit economics and financial accountability to translating strategy across sales, finance and analytics teams.

Sources indicate that 08:33 From CMO to CRO: What Changes When You Start Owning the Numbers? — Kathy’s move into revenue leadership changed how she looks at the business. She now works more closely with the CFO and analytics teams, pays closer attention to what can be dialed up or down and thinks much more deliberately about the top line, bottom line and everything in between. Her unexpected takeaway? She has become “a little obsessed with numbers.”.

18:42 If Sales Doesn’t Understand the Question, Ask It Differently — Leading a sales organization forced Kathy to rethink how she communicates. What sounds perfectly clear in marketing language may not land with sales at all. Her solution is simple: reframe the question through the listener’s lens. Small changes in language can create much better alignment across teams.

20:15 How “Edutainment” Breaks a Sea of Sameness — Home warranties require explanation, but explanation alone is easy to ignore, which is why Frontdoor’s answer is “edutainment,” combining category education with humor through its work with Rachel Dratch. Kathy claims the approach has helped American Home Shield differentiate itself while improving awareness, demand and conversion.

Industry observers note that 23:00 Your Audience Assumptions Can Expire Faster Than You Think — Frontdoor has historically wanted to reach younger homeowners, but rising home prices and changing buying patterns complicate that assumption. Kathy’s point for marketers is broader: consumer segments move. The job is to keep checking the data, challenge inherited audience assumptions and pivot when real behavior changes.

Jenny Rooney is Chief Brand and Community Officer, leading strategy for the overall ADWEEK brand as well as the ways in which we serve and support our audiences with high-value content, products, partnerships and experiences, notably through our community programs such as Marketing Vanguard.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Brands are expected to spend 10-30% more on digital media activity over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compared with 2025, according to five media buyers who spoke with Digiday.
  • Spending growth around Black Friday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Brands are expected to spend 10-30% more on digital media activity over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, compared with 2025, according to five media buyers who spoke with Digiday. Retail media, particularly Amazon, search, CTV and YouTube, are expected to soak up much of that increase.

Spending growth around Black Friday (Nov. 27) and Cyber Monday (Nov. 30), the twin peaks of the holiday season for many retailers, hardly comes as a surprise. According to Triple Whale, 33,000 U.S. brands spent $607 million across the Black Friday/Cyber Monday period last year; this year, Bain Capital estimates U.S. companies to record $85 billion in sales over the five day period, accounting for 8.5% of total holiday spending for 2026.

But there’s nuance to be considered, especially with retailers choosing to discount earlier in the year.

“We expect higher spend across direct-response channels this year, though it varies by category and brand,” mentioned Brett Fischer, associate director of performance media at e-commerce-focused media agency Collective Measures.

It has been revealed that for one, product discounting and marketing activity kicked off earlier this year. According to commerce media company Fluent, 32% of shoppers had already begun holiday purchases prior to Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the number of products listed at a discount between Oct. 1-20 rose 56%, and increased 71% during the week preceding Prime Substantial Deal Days, according to data from e-commerce company Wayvia. In 2025, the same discounting surge didn’t kick in until the middle of November.

That’s driven budget increases, or forced some marketers to spread their ad dollars over a longer period of time. Nola Ladd, associate director of brand media at Collective Measures, stated the agency’s clients had spread their ad dollars thinner over a longer period, with the aim of improving consumer consideration.

Recent findings suggest that “Mid-funnel investment is running roughly flat year over year,” stated Ladd. “Instead of growing it in this period, we’ve spread it across more of the year so brands are building consideration well before peak season.”.

In a recent development, U.S. retail sales are expected to rise 4.2% this year compared with 2025, according to Oxford Economics, while the National Retail Federation (NRF) estimated that 182.7 million Americans will shop during the five-day run of discounts and sales, a slight reduction from 2025’s 186.9 million.

For some retailers, heavy discounting in the run-up to Black Friday is beginning to bite. Data from media agency PMG found that weekly sales rose 10% during October’s Prime Significant Deal Days (staged by Amazon on Oct. 6-7), with grocery purchases increasing 37.7% in volume. But the average selling price in that category fell 13.1%, while electronics revenues were “flat.”.

“Many of our clients in CPG and home delivery are watching sell-through closely,” noted Scott Shamberg, president and CEO at media agency Mile Marker.

“Many of our clients saw softness for the last few weeks but are still expecting to see demand and sales pick up,” said Michelle Merklin, vp of search innovation and growth, Tinuiti.

Companies affected by tariff-related cost increases will have to choose between crucial profit margin or the need to match competitors’ discounts. “It’s important for brands to continue to stay competitive within this time frame,” said Carly Carson, head of integrated media at PMG.

Recent findings suggest that “Our clients’ spend this Black Friday and Cyber Monday is mixed — some are flat and some are up. There has been some softening in the market the last quarter, so some clients are being conservative,” said Josy Amann, co-founder, Ars X Machina (AXM).

Per PMG data, brands that discounted across a larger range of their portfolio enjoyed a lot more growth during October: on average, those with 75% of their product set on discount saw 16% overall revenue growth, while companies that discounted 25% or less of their products saw overall revenues fall 11%.

Sales softness, and increased cost of sales hasn’t led to clients risking a retreat from Black Friday spending — the weekend window is too crucial a sales event for retailers. “We have definitely been making strong recommendations around maintaining a full-funnel strategy… BFCM is a great time to find latest consumers in a shopping mindset,” noted Amann.

In a recent development, but some advertisers were shifting dollars into channels considered to be safer bets. “Less brand, more performance channels,” Shamberg explained. Merklin also stated Tinuiti clients were, on the whole, choosing not to cut media budgets.

Those safer bets include CTV and YouTube, as well as retail media options. According to Brock Berry, CEO of digital ad trafficking platform AdCellerant, the quantity of advertisers running CTV activity during November was 25% than the same period last year, despite CPMs running as much as 18% higher in some regions following high competition from political spenders during the midterm elections. Shamberg said he expected to see “double-digit growth” in each of those channels among Mile Marker clients.

At the same time, product discovery behaviors are under question. A survey of 29,000 consumers commissioned by delivery tech giant DHL estimated that 90% of shoppers used generative AI chatbots or assistants to compare prices, while half said they used the tools to browse.

Industry observers note that as such, marketers are paying close attention to search, Merklin noted. She noted Tinuiti clients were expected to spend 11 to 15% more with Google compared with last year, with total search spending up 11% versus 2025. Clients’ standalone display campaign spending had largely shifted into the tech giant’s Demand Gen and Performance Max campaigns, which rose 30% and both include display and video inventory.

Industry observers note that PMG’s Carson remarked clients were spending on social as well, with an eye to influencing product discovery, while also increasing CTV investments. “That’s an area where we expect investment to be up well into the double digits year-over-year,” she said.

Recent findings suggest that “[It’s] something I don’t see slowing down in 2027,” addedCarson. “More advanced targeting capabilities here, including around placing ads during specific content contexts, are going to make it easier for brands to further invest.”.

Meta’s reported CTV expansion and AppLovin’s alleged interest in Criteo are foreboding for independent ad tech as major platforms extend their reach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

This story was first published by Digiday sibling Glossy.

It has been revealed that gap Inc. posted its earnings results for the third quarter of 2026 on Thursday, with double-digit growth from the Gap brand offsetting declines from Athleta and Banana Republic.

“Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency and underlying health of the brand is giving us real confidence in the brand’s ability to continue its momentum,” mentioned Gap Inc. CEO Richard Dickson on Thursday’s earnings call. “Our customer file continues to grow, particularly as we attract newer Gen Z customers, but we’re doing it while we’re preserving the brand’s multi-generational appeal.”.

Sources indicate that gap’s net sales were up 11% to $1.1 billion, and Old Navy’s net sales rose 1% to $2.3 billion. Meanwhile, Athleta’s net sales fell 14% to $220 million, and Banana Republic declined 3% to $449 million. The company as a whole reported a 2% increase in net sales to $4 billion.

In a recent development, dickson cited additional introduces from Gap’s collaborations with Hailey Bieber and Victoria Beckham as boosting sales in the period, along with the brand’s reentry into the beauty category. The organization did not share specific figures from the revival of Gap’s classic ‘90s fragrances like Grass and Dream in July, but called the early response “encouraging.”.

The company is doubling down on creating what it calls “fashiontainment,” Dickson shared. Following the appointment of Pam Kaufman as evp, chief entertainment officer in January, Gap Inc. has tapped boy band Just Your Type (JYT) for a multi-year partnership and released “The Agency,” a scripted microseries made for Banana Republic. Looking ahead, Dickson remarked Gap will also co-produce a docuseries.

“We see our fashiontainment platform as a recognized way of how customers aren’t just buying apparel today; they’re buying into brands that are telling compelling stories and driving cultural conversations,” remarked Dickson.

The Rundown: BADBOX 3.0, the CTV ad fraud scheme generating 40 billion bid requests a day

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1051 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
  • Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.
  • Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Last week, HUMAN Security claimed it has disrupted the largest publicly disclosed ad fraud operation by bid-request volume, uncovering a network of infected streaming devices generating up to 40 billion fraudulent ad requests daily.

Dubbed “BADBOX 3.0,” the scheme accounted for more than 4% of CTV traffic observed by HUMAN, using compromised Android TV boxes to impersonate legitimate streaming apps and generate advertising activity without viewers’ knowledge.

The Nov. 18 disclosure raises fresh questions about the effectiveness of CTV ad fraud detection — and how much fraudulent inventory slips through existing safeguards, vital gaps for the industry to collectively plug as marketers increasingly spend ad dollars on such channels.

According to HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence team, the situation involved a network of compromised, low-cost Android-based streaming devices running malware designed to generate fraudulent video advertising activity without their owners’ knowledge.

The operation was more than three times larger, by peak daily bid-request volume, than VASTFLUX, previously the largest publicly disclosed scheme measured on that basis.

Researchers linked elements of the malware distribution infrastructure to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, identifying connections involving device software, code repositories and command-and-control servers.

HUMAN also uncovered links to earlier BADBOX operations, including BADBOX 2.0, which was exposed in 2025 and involved more than 10 million compromised devices across 222 countries and territories.

The latest discovery illustrates how fraud operations can reconstitute themselves following earlier disruptions, adapting their infrastructure and techniques to evade detection.

The malware then installed advertising software on infected devices, allowing video commercials to play in hidden windows while users continued watching television or navigating their streaming interfaces.

The resulting advertising requests impersonated legitimate CTV applications, making the inventory appear authentic to downstream buyers.

Some fraudulent requests also originated from residential proxy networks, helping disguise their source as ordinary household internet traffic.

HUMAN identified 11 proxy networks in which compromised devices could be enrolled without their owners’ consent, effectively turning consumer internet connections into infrastructure available for third-party use. Separately, researchers uncovered spoofed server-side ad insertion traffic, in which fraudulent requests purported to represent advertisements inserted into streaming sessions that did not actually exist.

The scale of the operation is considerable, although its financial impact remains unclear.

According to recent reports, crucially, the 40 billion figure represents bid requests, not completed advertising transactions or billable impressions. Consequently, it cannot be used to calculate advertiser losses without establishing how much fraudulent inventory was purchased.

Hence, the question remains: what proportion of the 40 billion daily bid requests became paid impressions? And how much money was spent on invalid inventory?

However, due to the intricacies of online ad auctions – where CPMs can vary significantly – HUMAN was unable to provide an exact dollar amount when asked about the financial impact of the operation.

Nonetheless, sources approached by Digiday estimated that BADBOX 3.0 could potentially have cost advertisers millions of dollars per day at its height.

It has been revealed that shailin Dhar, partner at Futureproof TMT, cautioned against equating the operation’s 40 billion daily bid requests with actual advertiser losses, noting that CTV supply audited by his firm since 2024 has averaged a fill rate of approximately 2%. He further counseled that fraudulent inventory originating from low-end applications and devices could perform considerably worse.

At this juncture, it’s worth considering that enormous volumes of fraudulent auction traffic do not necessarily translate into equivalent volumes of wasted advertising expenditure. At an illustrative fill rate of 0.5% and realized revenue of $3 per thousand impressions, 40 billion daily requests would generate approximately $600,000 in revenue. However, Dhar stressed that such calculations should not be mistaken for evidence of the operation’s actual earnings.

Nevertheless, the operation’s ability to masquerade as legitimate streaming inventory highlights potential weaknesses in how CTV advertising transactions are authenticated.

Sources indicate that CTV has become an increasingly important channel for advertisers seeking to reach audiences migrating from traditional television. However, its programmatic infrastructure also presents opportunities for fraudsters to exploit fragmented supply paths and inconsistent verification practices.

Industry observers note that BADBOX 3.0 demonstrates how apparently legitimate app identifiers, residential IP addresses and video ad requests can be combined to manufacture the appearance of genuine viewing activity. The question is whether existing safeguards can consistently identify such behavior before advertisers are charged.

Futureproof’s Dhar questioned the effectiveness of existing verification safeguards, arguing that private marketplaces and curated deals remain vulnerable because of limited device, content, and connection signals, alongside excessive confidence in identity matching.

“My personal estimate is roughly a 90% chance that at least one comparable operation is running without public identification,” he told Digiday, while acknowledging that its scale and financial impact remain unknown.

Per Dhar’s assessment, effective CTV verification requires persistent checks throughout the advertising supply chain, rather than relying exclusively on pre-bid or post-bid detection.

For now, HUMAN says customers using its Ad Fraud Defense service are protected against the operation’s associated attacks, while its researchers continue monitoring the perpetrators for further adaptations.

The findings come roughly a month after a separate investigation by ad security firm Confiant and researchers at Citizen Lab exposed how online advertising infrastructure was used to distribute spyware, highlighting another vulnerability in the digital advertising ecosystem.

That investigation, detailed in research published by Citizen Lab, found that Israeli tech giant Discover-Tech exploited targeted advertising mechanisms to deliver zero-click spyware, including attacks against devices at Al Jazeera.

While the two operations differed in their objectives — one targeting advertising budgets, the other facilitating surveillance — both illustrate how infrastructure designed to connect advertisers with audiences can be repurposed for malicious activity.

The broader concern is that BADBOX 3.0 is another iteration of an established threat rather than an isolated incident — and that dismantling one operation does not necessarily eliminate the infrastructure or incentives behind the next.

D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
  • This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
  • This is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

This is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies. The report is based on a survey of 90 brand and retailer professionals, as well as individual interviews with marketing executives.

Digiday’s survey found that brands and retailers proposal to adjust the marketing tactics they’ll use during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to those they used in 2025.

The biggest changes are that CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026, with year-over-year increases of 22 percentage points and 20 percentage points, respectively.

Industry observers note that forty-five percent of survey respondents said they strategy to use CTV/streaming ads this holiday season, in comparison to 23% of respondents who said the same in 2025. The 2026 uptick followed a 14 percentage point dip in usage from 2024 to 2025.Meanwhile, marketers’ usage of TV ads remained relatively stable between 2024 and 2025, dropping by only 4 percentage points between 2024 and 2025, but grew by a whopping 20 percentage points in 2026. Thirty-three percent of brands and retailers said they plan to use TV ads this holiday season in comparison to 13% of marketers who said the same in 2025.

Industry observers note that “Streaming is a really valid channel to invest in during holiday because consumption of that media spikes,” said Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement organization Ritual. “But participating in streaming is actually a decision for the whole year. Starting to engage just for holiday would be a risky move, especially for a smaller brand.”.

“If you have the data to back it up over the course of the year showing this is a channel that’s proven and the ROI metrics associated, it can make a lot of sense to spike it during holiday,” she added.

In a recent development, ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, stated that both streaming and TV ads can be effective for targeting specific demographic groups during the holidays. “Streaming and television is an effective audience conversion mechanism, especially with women over 30 years old,” Bloom said. “We’ve done a lot of work on daytime TV and on QVC. We see significantly bigger segments in the holiday time period from November through mid-December, and we always put attention on those times.”.

In a recent development, last year, brands’ and retailers’ most-used holiday marketing tactic was brand experiences, but that strategy fell to second place in 2026 behind streaming/CTV ads. Forty-one percent of marketers mentioned they expect to use brand experiences as a marketing strategy during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to 50% of marketers who said the same in 2025 — a drop of 9 percentage points.

According to recent reports, brands and retailers are also divesting from using gift guides and influencer hauls/unboxing videos this holiday season. Marketers’ usage of gift guides decreased by 19 percentage points in 2026 vs. 2025, while their use of influencer hauls/unboxing videos fell by 14 percentage points this year in comparison to last year.

Although gift guides and brand experiences decreased in marketer usage for the 2026 holidays, they remain brands’ and retailers’ top performing holiday marketing tactics over time. Thirty-one percent of marketers stated gift guides have historically performed the best for their tech giant during the holiday season, while 28% of marketers said the same of brand experiences, putting them in the No. 1 and No. 2 ranking spots, respectively.

Although some marketers are shifting away from using gift guides for the upcoming holiday season, Ritual’s Brodie said gift guides are likely to gain importance in the AI-driven search era because AI-powered search tools often rely on best of lists and curated recommendations to answer consumer queries.

It has been revealed that “Gift guides are very interesting in the world of AEO and thinking about LLM optimization,” Brodie said. “Overall, best of lists and gift guides are a close sister to [AI search results]. Gift guides can play an vital role in holiday and especially bridging LLM research and AI overviews. So, I’m bullish about gift guides.”.

Although brands and retailers are leaning into CTV/streaming ads for the 2026 holidays, those marketing tactics tied in the No. 4 spot for the best-performing holiday marketing tactic over time, while pop-up shops ranked No. 3. Influencer hauls/unboxing videos was the only marketing strategy that fell in both best historic performance and marketers’ intended use during the 2026 holiday season.

A-Frame Brands’ Bloom said brands and retailers should also consider investing in catalogs for the 2026 holiday. “Catalogs have always been very successful, and they’re heavily conversion-focused,” Bloom explained. “When they’re discount-driven and when people’s attention is on buying, you can do offers that you can only get via physical paper, and it does drive people into stores.”.

#181068. Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (845 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
  • Agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story.
  • Clients do not hire agencies to be fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Amol Waishampayan, co-founder, fullthrottle.ai.

Agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story. Faster work, leaner teams, lower fees. Clients took the meeting, nodded along and then waited for the invoice to shrink. It didn’t. AI strategies now sound interchangeable to clients, who say the savings never revealed up in their fees.

That is not an AI problem. It is a positioning problem. Efficiency was the wrong promise. Clients do not hire agencies to be fast. They hire them to grow the business. AI’s real opportunity for agencies is not doing the same work cheaper. It is doing work that actually moves revenue, and proving it.

It has been revealed that agencies are getting operational value from AI. According to the Digiday Media Agency Report 2026, 70% of agencies say AI has cut costs by making tasks more efficient, while 31% say it cost more to implement than expected. But efficiency is a one-time gain.

Once every agency has it, nobody gets paid for it. As one Gartner analyst told Digiday, the honeymoon between agencies and AI is “essentially over.” The agencies that build their AI story on productivity are competing on margin. The ones that build it on performance are competing on value, and value is what clients renew.

Most media plans are still organized by channel. Search budget here, social budget there, streaming over in a separate deck. AI makes that structure obsolete, because it can plan around the customer instead.

Take a regional home services company running paid search and social. Those campaigns are producing something more valuable than clicks: a live stream of households actively researching its services. AI can turn those signals into a defined first-party audience, figure out where else those households spend their time, and extend the initiative into streaming TV, digital video and audio to reach them there. One audience, coordinated across channels, built from the client’s own demand rather than a platform’s inventory.

That is a different kind of planning. The question stops being “what should we spend on CTV” and becomes “who are we trying to reach, and where are they?”.

Sources indicate that the next step is letting AI act on that intelligence. Agentic systems can take audience and performance signals and adjust targeting, channel mix and spend as conditions change, instead of waiting for the monthly optimization meeting. Static intends with quarterly reviews are a relic of how long it used to take humans to read the data.

But here is where agencies should be careful. The advantage is not how much of the buying you automate. Anyone can automate. The advantage is whether the agent is optimizing toward something that matters. An agent chasing cheaper CPMs will find them, and the client will not care. An agent optimizing toward the client’s actual business outcomes, with the agency keeping full transparency and control, is a different product entirely.

Sources indicate that this is the part most of the industry still avoids. Clicks and impressions are easy to report and nearly impossible to defend in a budget conversation. The only metrics a CFO cares about are sales, customers and revenue.

In a recent development, AI makes closing that gap practical. Bring together the advertiser’s first-party customer data, its transaction history and campaign exposure, and one can see which households were reached, which ones became customers and which channels and audiences did the work. Done with privacy-first, household-level methods rather than individual tracking, this is not surveillance. It is the client’s own data finally answering the client’s own question.

According to recent reports, once that loop exists, everything upstream improves. Planning gets smarter because it is fed by real conversions. Agentic buying gets better because it is optimizing toward revenue instead of proxies. And the agency walks into every renewal with proof rather than a deck.

Agencies are already monetizing AI. Digiday’s report found that 59% are launching new AI-powered products, 34% are selling strategic roadmaps or audits and 31% are charging additional fees for AI-powered services. But if the product is “we have AI,” the pricing power will not last. Every competitor has AI. Within a year, every client will have it too.

The agencies that win the next cycle will not be the ones with the most AI. They will be the ones who can show a client exactly what it delivered, in the client’s own numbers. Efficiency gets agencies a thank-you. Outcomes get agencies the next three years of the account.Partner insights from fullthrottle.ai.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.
  • Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.

Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work. These teams have their own agents, their own data and their own rules for what an agent may and may not do. At the same time, most of the specialized intelligence they depend on still sits inside separate vendor platforms.

As a result, vendor intelligence shapes a recommendation while remaining disconnected from the system acting on the recommendation. When planners carry conclusions between tools, the evidence and conditions behind those recommendations often fall away.

That’s the problem agentic media has to solve next. Can the intelligence behind the agent go where the work happens?

Models and agent frameworks are widely available. Two vendors can build on the same foundation and ship agents that look identical in a demo. What separates them is what the agent knows, and whether the advertiser can put that knowledge to work. In media buying, that knowledge is specific.

According to recent reports, A broad content classification offers only a starting point for a media decision. Suitability depends on the particular advertiser and market, and those judgments can change swiftly when breaking news alters the significance of a placement. A general-purpose model can’t reconstruct that brand-specific knowledge or historical context from a prompt alone. Classification depth and performance history can.

For Channel Factory, that means IAB 3.0 classification across more than 15 million YouTube channels, and more than 10 years and $4 billion of campaign performance data. To be clear, this isn’t an argument for keeping that intelligence locked inside a platform; it’s the opposite. Intelligence that only works inside its owner’s interface is as limited as a capable agent no one can reach.

In a recent development, so the test is portability. Can an advertiser’s own agent call on a provider’s intelligence directly, from inside the planning and buying environment it already uses? That’s how Channel Factory is building, with contextual and suitability intelligence made available through APIs and MCP servers, and delivered through modular agents that run inside an advertiser’s environment or alongside it.

It has been revealed that with this architecture, market-specific suitability analysis becomes part of an advertiser’s own planning process. An agent can evaluate inventory against the provider’s classifications and historical performance data, applying the relevant standards for each market. Those findings can directly inform the initiative, with the advertiser’s existing rules governing what the agent can recommend or change.

Industry observers note that portable intelligence doesn’t mean identical agents. Two advertisers can draw on the same underlying intelligence and make different decisions. For instance, one avoids content when signals are unclear while another favors reaching inside defined boundaries. Both are valid because the thresholds, priorities and approval rules are the advertisers’.

According to recent reports, an agent’s knowledge source shouldn’t determine the scope of its authority. The brand decides what acceptable judgment looks like. The provider keeps the classification, history and models current.

It has been revealed that learning needs the same discipline. Feedback and outcomes should refine recommendations, but advertisers should decide what shapes future decisions and which policies stay fixed. On its own, a successful campaign shouldn’t rewrite a brand’s suitability standards.

In a recent development, intelligence that moves into someone else’s systems has to carry its accountability along. As agents shift from recommending to acting, teams need to see what changed, why and whether it stayed within approved limits.

The principle is simple: Agents do the reasoning, and the engine owns the state, so every action is authorized, logged and traceable to the signals behind it. People define the strategy. Autonomy is earned in stages: alerts first, then recommendations, then bounded actions. An agent might make a small budget adjustment under set conditions while sending a larger change for human approval. How much authority to delegate is the advertiser’s call, and the system should make that call easy to enforce and easy to review.

According to recent reports, as agentic capabilities spread, feature lists will converge. Advertisers should look underneath the interface and put three questions to any provider:.

The providers who can answer those clearly will matter more as brands take greater control of how they buy media. The rest will be unrealized demos.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What should have been a slow news week with the Thanksgiving holiday approaching was turned on its head Monday morning, when news broke that Nvidia had reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.

This comes after Huang recently stepped down following revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

CNBC was one of the first networks to break the news at 8:56 a.m. ET, and was also the first to speak with President Donald Trump following the reinstatement.

This is the moment the Jensen Huang news broke on @CNBC: pic.twitter.com/YKrRxLt7Ul.

— Brian Stelter (@brianstelter) November 23, 2026.

Eamon Javers, CNBC’s senior Washington correspondent, was the one who initially talked to the president, telling TVNewser that Trump called him as he was headed to CNBC’s DC bureau.

In a follow-up to our recent 5 Questions For… series, which covered Huang’s unexpected departure, Javers details how he learned of the reinstatement, his conversation with the president, and the coordination involved with the control room.

How did you hear about the news of Jensen Huang’s return?

I was walking my daughter to her bus stop this morning, and my phone blew up with texts from our bureau. It’s maybe the most crucial business story of the year, and I was a little frustrated that I was out of position when it broke. So I began texting sources for comment.

TVNewser: How did the call with President Trump occur?

Javers: He called me as I was in my car on the way to our CNBC bureau. I wasn’t expecting it at all. But we have talked on the phone from time to time, and I had tried to reach him earlier in the morning for his comment. So, I pulled over on the side of the road, called my desk, and was able to patch into the control room for a live interview. The whole process took about 4 minutes, and then we went live for nearly an hour. Our producers, control room team, and anchors did an incredible job of rolling with it and reacting very, very promptly so we could make it happen.

TVN: What was it like to talk to the president in real time during such a unique moment?

Javers: It’s always an honor to talk to the president of the United States, and today it was a unique opportunity because there was so much that was unknown about the role he played behind the scenes. I was focused on all of the aspects that were still unknown, and trying to get the president to explain the who, what, when, and why of how this happened.

TVN: How were you coordinating the conversation with the newsroom and control room?

Sources indicate that javers: We didn’t coordinate it or prep in advance at all. It happened too quickly. And your audience will understand the technical aspect of this, which is that on a phoner, you can’t communicate with the control room during the interview. On TV, they can speak to you in your earpiece to communicate how long you have left, if the anchors want to get in a question, and all of the production stuff you need in real time. Here it was just — do it live.

TV: What are the business ramifications of such a re-appointment?

In a recent development, javers: We’ve really never seen anything this extraordinary in corporate America — at least in my lifetime. I think it’s too early to say how this will play out, and certainly too early to say whether it will be successful or not. One thing is for sure: This story isn’t over yet.

Recent findings suggest that mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.
